lessons.title: Introduction to Curtain Walls and Shopfronts
lessons.body: Curtain walls and shopfronts are large aluminum and glass systems that cover building facades or storefronts. Unlike windows, they don't support the building's weight; they hang off the structure. In Africa, these are common in malls, banks, and office buildings in cities like Nairobi, Lagos, and Johannesburg. To fabricate a basic shopfront, you'll need 2" x 4" aluminum tubes (or 50mm x 100mm), 6mm tempered glass, and gaskets. Start by measuring the opening accurately using a laser measure or steel tape. Cut the vertical mullions (uprights) and horizontal rails (transoms) with a mitre saw at 45-degree angles for corners. Use a router to cut weep holes for drainage. Assemble with corner cleats and stainless steel screws. For curtain walls, you need a pressure plate system: the glass sits on setting blocks, then a pressure plate compresses the gasket. A typical curtain wall panel is 1.5m wide by 3m high. You'll need a spider crane or a team of four to lift panels into place. Always check with a spirit level and plumb bob. In Africa, where temperatures can exceed 40Â°C, use thermal breaks (see Lesson 3) to prevent expansion issues. Safety: wear gloves, safety glasses, and harnesses when working at height. A successful shopfront installation can earn $50-$100 per square meter in labour, so mastering this opens lucrative contracts.

lessons.title: Fabricating Large Sliding Doors and Bi-Fold Doors
lessons.body: Large sliding doors and bi-fold doors are popular for patios, balconies, and open-plan living in African homes. A typical sliding door can be 3m wide and 2.4m high, using 2mm thick aluminum profiles. For sliding doors, you need top and bottom tracks, rollers, and a locking mechanism. Start by cutting the frame: verticals at 2.4m, horizontals at 1.5m each for a two-panel door. Use a mitre saw with a 45-degree blade for clean corners. Assemble with corner stakes and screws. Install rollers on the bottom of each panel; top rollers guide the panel. For bi-fold doors, you need a track system with hinges and pivots. A four-panel bi-fold might have two panels folding to each side. Cut panels at 600mm wide each. Use heavy-duty hinges every 600mm. In Africa, where dust and heat are issues, use nylon rollers instead of steel to reduce noise and wear. Test the door by sliding it back and forth; adjust rollers with a screwdriver until it moves smoothly. For large openings, add a mid-rail for strength. A well-made sliding door can cost $200-$400 in materials, and you can charge $500-$800 installed. Always use tempered glass for safety. If the door is wider than 2.4m, consider a bottom track with a drainage channel to prevent water pooling during rainy seasons.

lessons.title: Using Thermal Breaks for Energy Efficiency
lessons.body: Thermal breaks are barriers between the inside and outside of an aluminum frame that reduce heat transfer. In hot African climates, they keep cool air in and heat out, cutting air conditioning costs by up to 30%. A thermal break is typically a polyamide strip inserted between two aluminum profiles. To make a thermal-broken window, you need a 'thermal break' profile, which is two aluminum sections joined by a reinforced plastic strip. You can buy these profiles pre-made, or use a 'pour and debridge' method: pour polyurethane into a channel, let it cure, then cut away the aluminum bridge. For a small workshop, pre-made profiles are easier. When fabricating, cut and assemble as normal, but ensure the thermal break is not damaged. Use a thermal break saw blade (carbide-tipped) to avoid melting the plastic. Install low-E glass (with a metallic coating) to further improve efficiency. In Africa, where electricity is expensive, this is a selling point: tell customers they'll save on bills. Test with a thermal camera or simply touch the frame on a hot day: a thermal-broken frame will be cooler. Cost: thermal break profiles cost about 20-30% more than standard, but you can charge 40-50% more. For a typical 1.2m x 1.5m window, the extra cost is $20-$30, but the customer saves $100+ per year on cooling. Always seal gaps with silicone to prevent air leaks.

lessons.title: Automating Windows and Doors
lessons.body: Automation adds motors, sensors, and controls to windows and doors for convenience, security, and energy efficiency. In Africa, automated gates and windows are increasingly common in upscale homes and businesses. Start with simple automation: a motorized sliding gate or a window opener. For windows, you need a linear actuator (12V or 24V), a remote control, and a transformer. A basic kit costs $80-$150. Install the actuator on the window frame, connecting it to the sash with a bracket. Wire it to a control box with a receiver. Test the limit switches so it stops at full open and close. For doors, use a sliding door motor (e.g., for a 2m wide door, a 600kg capacity motor). Mount the motor on the top track, attach a belt or rack to the door. Add safety sensors (infrared beams) to prevent crushing. In Africa, power outages are common, so include a battery backup (12V 7Ah) and a solar panel (20W) to keep it running. Automation can also be integrated with smart home systems like Google Home or Alexa using Wi-Fi modules. For commercial buildings, automatic sliding doors with motion sensors are standard. Cost: a basic automated window costs $200-$300 installed; a sliding gate $500-$1000. Learn basic electrical wiring: use a multimeter to check voltage, and always fuse the circuit. Safety: never put fingers near moving parts during testing. Automation is a high-value skill that can double your income.

lessons.title: Expanding to Multiple Crews and Locations
lessons.body: Scaling from a one-man workshop to multiple crews and locations requires systems, trust, and cash flow management. In Africa, successful aluminum businesses often start in a garage and grow to serve several cities. First, document your processes: write step-by-step guides for measuring, cutting, assembling, and installing. Use a checklist for each job. Then hire and train apprentices. A good rule: one experienced fabricator can supervise two apprentices. Pay daily or weekly; in many African countries, daily pay is expected. For a new location, start with a small rented space ($100-$300 per month) and a pickup truck for deliveries. Buy tools in bulk to save: a mitre saw ($200), a drill ($50), and a welding machine ($300). Use a central workshop for cutting and a satellite assembly team for installations. Track jobs with a simple notebook or a free app like Trello. Cash flow: require 50% deposit before ordering materials, 40% on delivery, and 10% after installation. Keep a reserve for slow months. Insurance: get liability insurance for accidents. In Kenya, for example, a growing aluminum company might have crews in Nairobi, Mombasa, and Kisumu. Communication is key: use WhatsApp groups for daily updates. Don't expand too fast; add one crew every 6-12 months. A crew of four can install 10 windows per day. With three crews, you can handle large contracts like schools or hospitals. Always pay your workers fairly to reduce turnover.

lessons.title: Staying Updated with New Products and Trends
lessons.body: The aluminum industry changes fast: new profiles, finishes, and smart features appear yearly. To stay competitive in Africa, you must keep learning. Follow manufacturers like Hydro, SAPA, and local suppliers on social media. Attend trade shows such as the Big 5 Construct in Kenya or Nigeria. Subscribe to magazines like 'Aluminium International Today' or join online forums. Key trends: slimline profiles for minimal sightlines, matte black and bronze finishes, and integrated blinds between glass panes. Also, sustainability: recycled aluminum is growing. In Africa, where solar gain is high, low-E glass and thermal breaks are in demand. For automation, voice control and app-based systems are hot. To test new products, order samples and try them in your workshop. For example, try a new gasket that resists UV better. Network with other fabricators: join a local association. Use YouTube to watch installation videos. When you learn something new, train your crew. Keep a library of catalogs and price lists. Update your quotes with current material costs; aluminum prices fluctuate with global markets. A simple habit: spend 30 minutes each week reading industry news. This helps you advise customers on the best options and charge premium prices. For instance, if you master a new 'lift and slide' door system, you can charge 20% more. Remember, your reputation grows when you offer the latest solutions. Don't be afraid to experiment on small projects before offering to clients.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Scaling Up and Advanced Techniques in Aluminium Windows & Doors

This practical reference supports the RISE AFRICA Skills module Scaling Up and Advanced Techniques for the course Aluminium Windows & Doors. It is written for fabricators, installers, workshop owners and site supervisors who already handle standard windows and doors and now want to move into larger, more technical and more profitable work: curtain walls, shopfronts, large sliding and bi-fold doors, thermal breaks, automation, multi-crew operations and staying current with a fast-changing product market.

In most African markets â from Lagos and Accra to Nairobi, Johannesburg and Dar es Salaam â the aluminium fabrication sector is growing quickly because of urban construction, retail expansion, higher-end residential demand and the need for energy-conscious buildings. The businesses that win are not only those that can weld and install, but those that can price correctly, standardise production, manage multiple sites and guarantee quality. This module gives you the technical and commercial reference material to do that.

1. Curtain Walls and Shopfronts: The Commercial Gateway

Curtain walls are non-structural, self-supporting external cladding systems, usually made of aluminium framing with glass, that hang off the building structure. Shopfronts are simpler, ground-floor glazed systems for retail units. Both are high-value jobs that require accurate surveying, structural understanding and careful sequencing. In Africa, curtain wall and shopfront demand is concentrated in malls, banks, offices, hotels, hospitals and fuel-station forecourts.

Key technical points for fabrication and installation:

  • Design loads: wind load is the governing factor in many coastal and high-rise African cities (Mombasa, Dar es Salaam, Luanda, Cape Town). Check local wind speed maps and structural engineer requirements.
  • Movement: allow for thermal expansion, seismic movement and building deflection. Use slotted connections and expansion joints, not rigid welds to the slab.
  • Drainage: curtain wall systems are drained and ventilated. Weep holes, baffles and pressure-equalised chambers must be installed exactly as the system supplier details.
  • Glass: specify laminated, toughened or double-glazed units according to safety, thermal and acoustic requirements. In hot climates, solar-control glass reduces cooling load dramatically.
  • Anchors: use tested anchors into concrete or steel. In many African projects, anchor pull-out tests are required by the engineer.

2. Fabricating Large Sliding Doors and Bi-Fold Doors

Large sliders (2.4 m to 6 m openings) and bi-folds (up to 6 m or more) are common in high-end residential estates, guest houses and lodges across Africa. They are heavier, more sensitive to alignment and more profitable than standard windows. Mistakes are expensive: a poorly aligned 4 m slider will drag, leak and sag.

Practical rules:

  • Track support: the bottom track must be level and fully supported. On suspended slabs, use a continuous structural base, not spot shims.
  • Weight calculation: glass weight is roughly 2.5 kg per mÂ² per mm of thickness. A 6 mÂ² 10 mm toughened panel weighs about 150 kg. Rollers must be rated above this with a safety margin.
  • Reinforcement: long mullions and stiles need steel or aluminium inserts to resist wind and self-weight deflection.
  • Drainage: bottom tracks must have drainage slots and sill heights designed for local rainfall intensity.
  • Bi-fold stacking: plan the stack position, hinge direction and traffic door clearly on the shop drawing before fabrication.

3. Using Thermal Breaks for Energy Efficiency

Thermal breaks separate the inner and outer aluminium profiles with a non-conductive material (usually polyamide). This reduces heat transfer, condensation and cooling load. In hot African climates, thermal breaks matter most when the building is air-conditioned or when the client wants lower energy bills. In cooler highland regions (Nairobi, Addis Ababa, Johannesburg winter), they reduce heating demand and condensation.

Commercial note: thermal break systems cost more in materials and require different fabrication (crimping or rolling the polyamide strip). Price them as a premium product, not a default, unless the specification demands it. Many African projects now require U-values or green-building certification (EDGE, IFC, Green Star SA), which makes thermal breaks a sales advantage.

4. Automating Windows and Doors

Automation is growing in Africa for security, accessibility, smoke ventilation and high-end residential convenience. Common systems include automatic sliding doors for malls and hospitals, motorised windows for smoke exhaust, and smart home integration.

Key considerations:

  • Power reliability: always specify battery backup or manual override. Grid interruptions are common.
  • Safety sensors: automatic doors must have presence and motion sensors to prevent injury.
  • Integration: choose systems that work with local voltages (220â240 V, 50 Hz) and are serviceable locally.
  • Warranty and spares: importers should stock motors, controllers and sensors. A door that cannot be repaired becomes a liability.

5. Expanding to Multiple Crews and Locations

Scaling from one crew to several is a business systems problem, not just a technical one. The fabricators who succeed standardise drawings, cutting lists, quality checks and site reporting. They also separate fabrication from installation so that crews can work in parallel.

Recommended operating model:

  • Central fabrication hub with fixed machinery and trained cutters.
  • Mobile installation crews (3â5 people) with their own tools, vehicles and checklists.
  • Site supervisor responsible for measuring, snagging and client sign-off.
  • Storekeeper controlling profiles, glass, gaskets and hardware to prevent theft and waste.
  • Weekly production meeting to review jobs, cash flow and quality issues.

6. Staying Updated with New Products and Trends

Aluminium systems change fast: new thermal break profiles, slim sightlines, concealed hardware, smart glass, solar shading and low-E coatings. African fabricators can stay current through supplier training, trade fairs (Big 5 Construct, Africa Build), manufacturer technical manuals and online catalogues. The businesses that invest in learning win the specification work.

Data Table 1: Comparative Performance of Window and Door Systems

System Typical Max Span Relative Cost Thermal Performance Best Use in Africa

Large sliding door 2.4â6.0 m Medium Moderate Lodges, villas, restaurants

Stick curtain wall Full building height High ModerateâHigh Offices, malls, hotels, hospitals
Thermally broken system Same as base system High High Air-conditioned, green-certified buildings

Source: compiled from manufacturer technical manuals (e.g. Hydro Building Systems â Technal Product Catalogue, Alumil â Architectural Aluminium Systems) and the Glass and Glazing Federation (GGF) Technical Guidance. Spans and costs are indicative and must be verified with the selected system supplier.

Data Table 2: Scaling Readiness Checklist for Fabrication Businesses

Area Single Crew Multi-Crew Ready Action
Drawings Verbal / sketches Standard shop drawings Use CAD templates for windows, sliders, curtain walls
Cutting One operator Cutting list + QC sheet Introduce cut optimisation and first-off checks
Installation Owner on site Trained supervisors Write installation method statements

Quality Visual Checklist + snag list Sign off before invoicing

Safety Basic PPE + toolbox talks Document incidents and near-misses

Source: adapted from the ILO â Safety and Health in Construction guidance and common practice in African aluminium fabrication SMEs.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Glass Handling, Lifting and Curtain Wall Installation

Large glass panels, curtain wall units and automated doors are heavy and dangerous. In African site conditions, the biggest risks are manual lifting, unstable scaffolding, unsecured panels in wind, and lack of PPE. Always use mechanical lifting equipment (vacuum lifters, hoists, scissor lifts) for panels above 50 kg. Never lift glass by hand above shoulder height. Secure all panels against wind before leaving site. Use cut-resistant gloves, safety boots, helmets and eye protection. Ensure scaffolding is inspected and tagged. Train every crew member on emergency response and first aid. A single dropped curtain wall panel can kill â no deadline justifies unsafe lifting.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Survey twice, fabricate once: measure openings, levels, plumb and structural openings before cutting.
  2. Confirm system and glass specification: wind load, thermal break, safety glass, U-value and colour.
  3. Check anchor and fixing design: pull-out capacity, edge distance, corrosion protection.
  4. Verify drainage and ventilation: weep holes, baffles, sill heights, gaskets and sealants.
  5. Use lifting equipment for heavy panels: vacuum lifters, hoists or crane; never manual lift above 50 kg.
  6. Sign off quality before invoicing: operation, alignment, locking, sealing, snag list closed.
  7. Document every job: drawings, cutting lists, delivery notes, installation photos, warranty.
  8. Train crews continuously: new products, safety, automation, thermal systems and customer care.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • Glass and Glazing Federation (GGF) â Free Technical Publications â curtain walling, glass and glazing guidance.
  • ILO â Safety and Health in Construction â free code of practice for site safety.
  • IFC EDGE â Excellence in Design for Greater Efficiencies â free green building certification and energy efficiency guidance for Africa.
  • ASHRAE â Free Technical Resources â thermal comfort, ventilation and energy standards.
  • South African Bureau of Standards (SABS) â relevant standards for glazing, aluminium and construction in Southern Africa.

Prepared for RISE AFRICA Skills â Aluminium Windows & Doors, Module: Scaling Up and Advanced Techniques. Always verify local building codes, wind loads, seismic requirements and supplier data before fabrication and installation.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between a curtain wall and a regular window?
options: A) Curtain walls are made of wood
B) Curtain walls do not support the building's weight
C) Curtain walls are only for residential use
D) Curtain walls are always smaller
quiz.explanation: Curtain walls hang off the structure and do not carry structural loads, unlike load-bearing walls.

quiz.q: Which tool is essential for cutting aluminum profiles at 45-degree angles?
quiz.explanation: A mitre saw with a carbide blade provides clean, accurate 45-degree cuts for corner joints.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of weep holes in a shopfront frame?
options: A) To allow water to drain
quiz.explanation: Weep holes allow condensation and rainwater to escape, preventing water damage.

quiz.q: For a large sliding door, what type of rollers are recommended in dusty African conditions?
quiz.explanation: Nylon rollers are more resistant to dust and reduce noise compared to steel rollers.

quiz.q: In a bi-fold door, how many panels typically fold to each side in a four-panel system?
quiz.explanation: A four-panel bi-fold door usually has two panels folding to the left and two to the right.

quiz.q: What is a thermal break in aluminum windows?
options: A) A gap filled with air
B) A plastic or polyamide barrier between inner and outer aluminum
C) A type of glass coating
quiz.explanation: A thermal break is a non-conductive material that separates the interior and exterior aluminum to reduce heat transfer.

quiz.q: How much can thermal breaks reduce air conditioning costs?
quiz.explanation: Thermal breaks can cut cooling costs by up to 30% by reducing heat gain.

quiz.q: Which method is used to create a thermal break by pouring polyurethane?
quiz.explanation: The pour and debridge method involves pouring polyurethane into a channel and then cutting away the aluminum bridge.

quiz.q: What type of glass is recommended to further improve energy efficiency with thermal breaks?
quiz.explanation: Low-E glass has a metallic coating that reflects heat, enhancing thermal performance.

quiz.q: What is the typical voltage for a linear actuator used in window automation?
quiz.explanation: Most window automation actuators operate on 12V or 24V DC for safety and compatibility with battery backups.

quiz.q: Why is a battery backup important for automated doors in Africa?
options: B) To keep working during power outages
quiz.explanation: Frequent power outages in many African regions make battery backup essential for continuous operation.

quiz.q: Which safety feature should be added to automated sliding doors?
quiz.explanation: Infrared sensors prevent crushing, and manual override allows operation during emergencies.

quiz.q: What is a common smart home system that can integrate with automated windows?
quiz.explanation: Google Home (and Alexa) can control automated windows via Wi-Fi modules.

quiz.q: When expanding to multiple crews, what is a recommended pay structure in many African countries?
quiz.explanation: Daily pay is common and expected in many African informal and semi-formal work arrangements.

quiz.q: How much deposit should you require before ordering materials for a job?
quiz.explanation: A 50% deposit covers material costs and reduces risk of non-payment.

quiz.q: What is a good rule for crew size when hiring apprentices?
options: A) One experienced fabricator per apprentice
B) One experienced fabricator per two apprentices
C) Two experienced fabricators per apprentice
quiz.explanation: One experienced fabricator can effectively supervise two apprentices for quality and safety.

quiz.q: Which app is recommended for tracking jobs in a growing aluminum business?
quiz.explanation: Trello is a free, simple project management tool suitable for tracking jobs.

quiz.q: How often should you add a new crew when expanding?
quiz.explanation: Adding one crew every 6-12 months allows for sustainable growth and proper training.

quiz.q: What is a key trend in aluminum profiles for modern architecture?
quiz.explanation: Slimline profiles provide minimal sightlines and are in high demand for contemporary designs.

quiz.q: Which trade show is mentioned for Africa?
quiz.explanation: Big 5 Construct is a major construction trade show held in Kenya and Nigeria.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of recycled aluminum?
quiz.explanation: Recycled aluminum reduces environmental impact and supports sustainability trends.

quiz.q: How can you test if a thermal break is working?
options: A) Touch the frame on a hot day
quiz.explanation: A thermal camera or touch test can show temperature difference; a thermometer gives precise reading.

quiz.q: What is the typical cost increase for thermal break profiles compared to standard?
quiz.explanation: Thermal break profiles cost about 20-30% more, but allow higher selling prices.

quiz.q: For a sliding door motor, what capacity is needed for a 2m wide door?
quiz.explanation: A 600kg capacity motor is typical for a 2m wide sliding door to ensure smooth operation.

quiz.q: What is a common problem with steel rollers in sliding doors?
quiz.explanation: Steel rollers can rust, are noisy, and wear out faster than nylon in dusty conditions.

quiz.q: What is the recommended glass thickness for a shopfront?
quiz.explanation: 6mm tempered glass is commonly used for shopfronts for strength and safety.

quiz.q: What is a key financial practice when scaling up?
options: A) Keep all cash in one account
quiz.explanation: Requiring deposits ensures cash flow for materials and reduces risk.

quiz.q: Which of these is a new product trend in aluminum windows?
quiz.explanation: Integrated blinds between glass panes are a growing trend for convenience and cleanliness.

quiz.q: How often should you spend time learning about new products?
options: D) Only when a customer asks
quiz.explanation: Spending 30 minutes weekly keeps you updated without overwhelming your schedule.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of joining a local fabricator association?
quiz.explanation: Associations provide networking, training, and industry updates.
